title: Choosing STL Containers
summary: The standard library offers **sequence** containers (ordered by position), **associative** containers (sorted by key), **unordered** containers (hash tables) and **adaptors** (stack, queue, priority queue). Default to `std::vector`, and switch only when a specific operation needs to be faster.
markdown:
## The families ```mermaid flowchart TD STL["Standard containers"] --> SEQ["Sequence"] STL --> ASSOC["Ordered associative
(balanced tree)"] STL --> UNORD["Unordered associative
(hash table)"] STL --> ADAPT["Adaptors"] STL --> VIEW["Views (non-owning)"] SEQ --> v["vector"] & a["array"] & d["deque"] & l["list"] & fl["forward_list"] ASSOC --> s["set, multiset"] & m["map, multimap"] UNORD --> us["unordered_set"] & um["unordered_map"] ADAPT --> st["stack"] & q["queue"] & pq["priority_queue"] VIEW --> sp["span"] & sv["string_view"] ``` | Family | Elements are organised by | Members | |---|---|---| | **Sequence** | Position: where you put them | `vector`, `array`, `deque`, `list`, `forward_list` | | **Ordered associative** | Key, kept sorted | `set`, `map`, and their `multi` forms | | **Unordered associative** | Key, by hash | `unordered_set`, `unordered_map` | | **Adaptors** | A restricted interface over another container | `stack`, `queue`, `priority_queue` | ## How each is laid out in memory The layout explains the performance. ``` vector [■■■■■■■■□□□] one contiguous block, with spare capacity deque [■■■■] [■■■■] [■■■■] fixed-size chunks: cheap growth at BOTH ends list ■ ⇄ ■ ⇄ ■ ⇄ ■ separately allocated nodes, each linked to its neighbours set / map ■ a balanced binary tree, / \ always in sorted order ■ ■ unordered [0] → ■ → ■ an array of buckets; [1] → (empty) the hash of a key picks the bucket [2] → ■ ``` ## Complexity | Operation | `vector` | `deque` | `list` | `set` / `map` | `unordered_set` / `map` | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Access by index | O(1) | O(1) | No | No | No | | Insert or remove at the end | O(1) amortized | O(1) | O(1) | | | | Insert or remove at the front | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | | | | Insert or remove in the middle | O(n) | O(n) | O(1), given the position | O(log n) | O(1) average | | Find by value or key | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(log n) | O(1) average | | Kept in sorted order | No | No | No | Yes | No | | Friendly to the processor's cache | Very | Fairly | No | No | Partly | Big-O ([[5.11 Sorting, Searching, Big-O and Timing Your Code]]) is not the whole story. It counts steps and says nothing about how long a step takes. Following a pointer to a node somewhere else in memory can be a hundred times slower than reading the next element of an array. > [!tip] A vector often beats a list where theory says it should not > Inserting in the middle of a `std::list` is O(1) and in a `std::vector` it is O(n). Yet for small and medium sizes the vector usually wins, because shifting contiguous elements is fast and reaching the insertion point in a list is not. Measure before switching: [[13.04 Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design]]. ## Choosing ```mermaid flowchart TD Q1{"Do you look things up
by a KEY?"} -- yes --> Q2{"Do you need the keys
in sorted order?"} Q2 -- yes --> MAP["std::map / std::set"] Q2 -- no --> UMAP["std::unordered_map /
std::unordered_set"] Q1 -- no --> Q3{"Is the size fixed
at compile time?"} Q3 -- yes --> ARR["std::array"] Q3 -- no --> Q4{"Do you add or remove
at the FRONT often?"} Q4 -- yes --> DQ["std::deque"] Q4 -- no --> Q5{"Do you always want the
largest or smallest next?"} Q5 -- yes --> PQ["std::priority_queue"] Q5 -- no --> VEC["std::vector
(the default)"] ``` `std::list` is absent from the chart on purpose. Its real advantages are narrow: iterators and references to its elements stay valid through insertions and removals elsewhere, and whole sections can be moved between lists in constant time. Choose it for those, not for speed. ## Iterator invalidation Which operations invalidate iterators, pointers and references into the container is part of each container's contract, and a frequent source of bugs. | Container | Insertion invalidates | Erasure invalidates | |---|---|---| | `vector` | Everything, if it reallocates; otherwise from the insertion point on | From the erased element on | | `deque` | All iterators | All iterators, unless at an end | | `list`, `set`, `map` | Nothing | Only the erased element | | `unordered_*` | All iterators, if it rehashes | Only the erased element | ## Adaptors An **adaptor** wraps another container and exposes only the operations of a particular data structure. ```cpp #include #include #include #include int main() { std::stack stack{}; // last in, first out stack.push(1); stack.push(2); std::cout << stack.top() << '\n'; // 2 std::queue queue{}; // first in, first out queue.push(1); queue.push(2); std::cout << queue.front() << '\n'; // 1 std::priority_queue largestFirst{}; largestFirst.push(5); largestFirst.push(9); largestFirst.push(2); std::cout << largestFirst.top() << '\n'; // 9 std::priority_queue, std::greater<>> smallestFirst{}; smallestFirst.push(5); smallestFirst.push(9); smallestFirst.push(2); std::cout << smallestFirst.top() << '\n'; // 2 return 0; } ``` | Adaptor | Order | Default underlying container | |---|---|---| | `std::stack` | LIFO | `deque` | | `std::queue` | FIFO | `deque` | | `std::priority_queue` | Largest first | `vector`, arranged as a heap | A priority queue gives O(log n) insertion and removal with O(1) access to the top. As with the vector-based stack, `pop()` returns nothing: read `top()` or `front()` first. ## A shared interface Nearly every container provides `size()`, `empty()`, `clear()`, `begin()` and `end()`, `insert`, `erase`, `emplace`, `swap` and comparison operators. That uniformity is why one algorithm works across all of them, and why switching container later is usually a small change. Hide the choice behind a type alias and it is a one-line change.
ideas:
1. Implement a waiting room with a `std::queue<std::string>`.
2. Use a `std::priority_queue` with a custom comparator to process the most urgent `Task` first.
3. Time inserting 100,000 integers at the front of a vector, a deque and a list.

cards.q: What is the default container, and why?
cards.a: `std::vector`: its contiguous storage is cache-friendly and fast for most operations.

cards.q: Which containers give O(1) average lookup by key?
Why can a vector beat a list for insertion in the middle?
cards.a: Its contiguous memory makes both finding the position and shifting elements fast, while a list has to follow scattered pointers.

cards.q: What does a container adaptor do?
cards.a: It wraps another container and exposes only the interface of a specific data structure, such as a stack or queue.
